title: 2 Chronicles 34:1–13
context: Josiah seeks the God of David in his eighth year and begins purging Judah, Jerusalem, and the northern territories in his twelfth year, before the temple repairs of his eighteenth year. In 2 Kings 22–23 the reforms are narrated after the book is found in the eighteenth year; the two accounts place them differently, and that difference is named here, not harmonized.

verses.text: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah begins to reign at eight and reigns thirty-one years. Arminian readers see a young king who will choose faithfulness, as the following verses describe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God raising up a faithful king after Amon. The account parallels 2 Kings 22:1, though the Chronicler omits the name of Josiah’s mother.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, and walked in the ways of David his father, and didn’t turn away to the right hand or to the left.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah “did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, and walked in the ways of David his father.” Arminian readers see wholehearted faithfulness freely pursued.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the same commendation given in 2 Kings 22:2. The phrase “didn’t turn away to the right hand or to the left” describes steady devotion.

verses.text: For in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David his father; and in the twelfth year he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem from the high places, the Asherah poles, the engraved images, and the molten images.
verses.arminianNotes: In his eighth year Josiah “began to seek after the God of David his father,” and in his twelfth year began to purge Judah and Jerusalem. Arminian readers see a young king’s growing devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God at work in Josiah from his youth. Chronicles places the start of the reforms here, before the book is found in the eighteenth year, while 2 Kings 23:4–20 narrates them after the finding; the difference is noted, not harmonized.

verses.text: They broke down the altars of the Baals in his presence; and he cut down the incense altars that were on high above them. He broke the Asherah poles, the engraved images, and the molten images in pieces, made dust of them, and scattered it on the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.
verses.arminianNotes: They break down the altars of the Baals and scatter the dust on the graves of those who sacrificed to them. Arminian readers see decisive action against idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see thorough reform. Similar actions appear in 2 Kings 23:4–14, where they follow the reading of the book, and readers in this tradition note the different placement without resolving it.

verses.text: He burned the bones of the priests on their altars, and purged Judah and Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “He burned the bones of the priests on their altars, and purged Judah and Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see the defilement of idolatrous altars so they could not be reused.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fulfillment of the word in 1 Kings 13:2, recorded in 2 Kings 23:16–20. The Chronicler records the action briefly as part of the early reforms.

verses.text: He did this in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, even to Naphtali, around in their ruins.
verses.arminianNotes: He does this in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali, “around in their ruins.” Arminian readers see reform extending into the former northern territories.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Josiah’s zeal reaching beyond Judah. 2 Kings 23:15–20 describes reforms in the north as well, and the precise sense of “in their ruins” is held cautiously.

verses.text: He broke down the altars, beat the Asherah poles and the engraved images into powder, and cut down all the incense altars throughout all the land of Israel, then returned to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: He breaks the altars, beats the Asherah poles and images to powder, and cuts down the incense altars “throughout all the land of Israel.” Arminian readers see a comprehensive purge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reform completed before the return to Jerusalem. The phrase “all the land of Israel” stresses the Chronicler’s concern for the whole people of God.

verses.text: Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had purged the land and the house, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz the recorder to repair the house of the LORD his God.
verses.arminianNotes: In his eighteenth year, “when he had purged the land and the house,” Josiah sends officials to repair the LORD’s house. Arminian readers see reform leading naturally to restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the temple repair following the purge. 2 Kings 22:3 names only Shaphan, while the Chronicler adds Maaseiah and Joah, a difference noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: They came to Hilkiah the high priest and delivered the money that was brought into God’s house, which the Levites, the keepers of the threshold, had gathered from the hands of Manasseh, Ephraim, of all the remnant of Israel, of all Judah and Benjamin, and of the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: They deliver money gathered by the Levites “from the hands of Manasseh, Ephraim, of all the remnant of Israel, of all Judah and Benjamin.” Arminian readers see broad participation in restoring God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Chronicler emphasizing contributions from north and south. The list reflects the book’s concern for all Israel, not Judah alone.

verses.text: They delivered it into the hands of the workmen who had the oversight of the LORD’s house; and the workmen who labored in the LORD’s house gave it to mend and repair the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The money goes to the overseers and workmen “to mend and repair the house.” Arminian readers see practical stewardship serving the restoration of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see careful administration, as in 2 Kings 22:5. The repair work provides the setting for the discovery of the book.

verses.text: They gave it to the carpenters and to the builders to buy cut stone and timber for couplings, and to make beams for the houses which the kings of Judah had destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes: They buy stone and timber for “the houses which the kings of Judah had destroyed.” Arminian readers see damage caused by unfaithful kings being repaired by a faithful one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see restoration reversing previous neglect. The phrase implicitly recalls the reigns of Manasseh and Amon, though the text does not name them.

verses.text: The men did the work faithfully. Their overseers were Jahath and Obadiah the Levites, of the sons of Merari; and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to give direction; and others of the Levites, who were all skillful with musical instruments.
verses.arminianNotes: “The men did the work faithfully,” overseen by Levites, some “skillful with musical instruments.” Arminian readers see integrity and skill joined in God’s service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Levites directing the work. The Chronicler’s mention of musicians among the overseers reflects his interest in Levitical roles, which 2 Kings 22 does not mention.

verses.text: Also they were over the bearers of burdens, and directed all who did the work in every kind of service. Of the Levites, there were scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites oversee burden-bearers and serve as scribes, officials, and gatekeepers. Arminian readers see many kinds of service contributing to a common task.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the orderly organization of the work. Readers in this tradition value the reminder that administrative and manual work alike serve God’s house.
